newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks expected to open lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks expected to open lower.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to move lower at the opening amid investor anxiety ahead of a slew of economic data due this week and the November 5 U.S. presidential election.
Analysts said the third quarter employee cost index, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, would be closely watched for any indication of rising labor costs.
"You had a bad day yesterday, futures are lower and there is too much uncertainty for anyone to step up to the plate," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities.
He said the market would continue to drift as investors wait for the data and the election.
The employee cost index, an inflation indicator closely followed by the Federal Reserve, is expected to rise 0.8 percent for the second quarter in a row.

"When people talk about inflation they usually mean oil or food and they are missing the point," Wachtel said. "The biggest component in the Consumer Price Index is labor. When labor costs get out of control you have inflation."
In Tokyo the Nikkei Average closed up 73 points at 20,958.
In London the FTSE 100 Index was down 36 points at 3989.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, American Express Co was down 1/4 at 46 after reporting earnings in line with market expectations following the New York Stock Exchange close on Monday.
Mobil Corp was down 1/4 at 117-1/8 and International Business Machines Corp fell 1/4 to 126-7/8. Ford Motor Co was off 1/8 at 31-1/8 and Chrysler Corp fell 1/8 to 33-3/8.
U.S. Treasuries were mixed, with the long bond down 1/32 to yield 6.84 percent.
The dollar was off its highs in Tokyo and beneath 1.51 marks in Europe.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said investors are trying to find the company that will have the ultimate toy for the Christmas season, but some toymakers are not listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
The New York Times's Market Place column said cash flow into mutual funds is slowing amid investor nervousness, fewer retirement plan contributions, and stock market uncertainty.
